tagline.text: A forest lake, zoo and family park in the heart of Pasig

location.label: Location
location.text: F. Legaspi Street, Maybunga, Pasig City

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100–1,000 (per person, depending on facilities used)

children.text: This urban forest park of roughly 7 to 8 hectares sits in Barangay Maybunga, Pasig City. With a man-made lagoon, botanical garden, butterfly pavilion, zoo, zipline and wall climbing, it suits family outings, and since 2023 it has been protected as a permanent forest park.

Pasig Rainforest Park is an urban forest stretching along F. Legaspi Street in Barangay Maybunga, in Pasig City on the eastern side of Metro Manila. Locals also call it Maybunga Rainforest Park, and it is known as RAVE (Rainforest Adventure Experience), a name given during its 2013 makeover. Residential areas lie to the west, while West Bank Road and the Manggahan Floodway are close to the east, so it is an easy drive from Ortigas Center.

The park's history goes back to 1977. It first opened to the public on about 4.8 hectares, and roughly 2.1 hectares were added in 1996. As the city grew, the mayor himself has said that a large part of the forest was lost to buildings and tree cutting. For that reason Pasig City designated the park a permanent forest park by ordinance in 2023, so that it cannot shrink any further. Reports give the current area anywhere from about 6.8 to 8 hectares, so this guide says roughly 7 to 8 hectares. In July 2023, to mark the city's 450th anniversary, Pasig held a planting event of 450 seedlings in the park. The mayor has called it one of the last forests left in the city and has repeatedly said he intends to protect it. New facilities have therefore focused on repairing older ones within the existing grounds rather than clearing more forest, and that approach has continued since 2024. For travelers, it helps to know that this is an everyday neighborhood park rather than a large resort-style amusement park, so expectations should be set accordingly.

Inside you will find a man-made lagoon, a botanical garden, a butterfly pavilion, a maze garden, an open-air amphitheater, a small zoo, swimming pools and adventure facilities. Rather than expecting dramatic scenery like a typical Philippine tourist spot, appreciate it as one of the few city green spaces where you can walk in the shade without air conditioning. It is especially good for families who live in Manila or have a free day in their schedule. The park has several names, which can be confusing when asking for directions. In the Grab app it often appears as "Pasig Rainforest Park," "Maybunga Rainforest Park" or "RAVE Park," so rather than settling on one, try searching all three. Look for the entrance on the F. Legaspi Street side. Pasig City Science High School is also located inside the park, so on weekday mornings you may see students in uniform passing through.
Fees and opening hours differ between sources or are out of date, so this guide does not give exact figures. Be sure to check the park's official announcements and latest notices before you visit.

You can ride a boat on the man-made lagoon in the middle of the park. A walking path runs along the water, which makes for a relaxed stroll with children. Many locals fish or rest along the edge, so weekend mornings are quite lively. Boat rides are sometimes suspended because of weather or maintenance, so check the notices on site.
Flower beds, a flower garden and the butterfly pavilion lie one after another. The butterfly pavilion has charged a separate admission in the past, so please confirm on site.

There is an aviary, a vivarium and a petting area where you can touch the animals. It is small, which suits young children. A small train that circles the park has also been reported, which helps if you have a child or an older relative who tires easily. Check on site whether it is running and what it costs.
There is a zipline about
high and about
long, plus wall climbing, rappelling and obstacle courses. These are risky activities, so check the safety rules and age limits on site.
The park is described as having an adult pool, kids' pools, a mini Olympic-size pool and an area with water slides. Whether they are open and what they cost varies by period, so check in advance.

The park has old balete (banyan) trees, and reports say the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) recognized a heritage tree and a marker was installed. The tangled roots are impressive, so take a photo in front of the tree. Do not touch or climb the branches or roots; just look.
In early 2024 the city presented 12 new facilities, including a senior citizens' park, a pet park and a kiddie playland. There is something to enjoy even when your group spans several ages.

The park has a full-size open-air amphitheater that hosts performances and local events. Even on days without events, the steps are a good place to rest, and the nearby lawn is used for picnics. The promenade area near the entrance has a function hall where weddings and birthdays are sometimes held.

items.title: Half-day family route
items.subtitle: From a morning walk to a wrap-up before lunch

children.text: Enter through the main gate and walk toward the lagoon, enjoying the shade of the trees. Early in the day many local residents are out jogging.
Look around the botanical garden and the butterfly pavilion. Butterflies are more active once the sun starts to come out.
Visit the zoo and the aviary, and if you have children, spend time at the playground.
If you are interested, try the zipline or wall climbing. Check on the day whether they are available.
Have lunch at a rest area in the park or a nearby restaurant, then call it a day.

It is easier to finish outdoor activities in the morning, before the heat. With children, do not try to cover everything; pick two or three places that interest you and enjoy them at a relaxed pace. After lunch the humidity rises and you tire quickly even in the shade.

items.title: A full day combined with Ortigas
items.subtitle: City shopping and a forest walk

children.text: Spend one to two hours walking and doing some light sightseeing in the park.
Take a Grab or taxi to Ortigas Center for lunch and shopping.
If you have time, you can continue to Eastwood City or toward Marikina.
From Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA) a Grab or taxi takes about
1 to 1.5 hours
. Avoid weekday rush hours, when traffic is heavy.
From central Manila the park connects via Ortigas Avenue, Raymundo Avenue, West Bank Road and Circumferential Road 5 (C-5).
Exact travel times vary greatly with the time of day.
No jeepney or bus route that goes directly to the park has been confirmed. In Pasig, tricycles and Grab are the usual choices.
Tricycles may charge a separate "special" fare if you ride alone, so confirm the fare before you get in.
The best time to go is on a dry-season morning, November to May. Because it is a leafy place, it is cooler even at midday than other city parks, but April and May are very hot.
In the rainy season, sudden afternoon downpours are common and outdoor adventure facilities may close. On weekends and holidays many local families visit and it can get crowded.

Around December there are often Christmas decorations and family events, so it can be busier than usual. If you want a quiet walk, weekday mornings between 8 and 10 in the dry season are most pleasant. Late in the afternoon the shade lengthens but mosquitoes increase, so use repellent.

There are few places to stay in or right next to the park, so most visitors stay at hotels around Ortigas Center or Bonifacio Global City (BGC) and come for a day trip. Pasig itself also has budget and mid-range hotels.
The park may have simple stores or food stalls, but their operation varies by period. Bring water and snacks, and for meals it is easier to use the restaurants in Ortigas or a nearby mall.

Most Korean travelers go back and forth by Grab from hotels in Ortigas or BGC. If it is hard to book a return ride in advance, it is easier to take a tricycle from the park exit to a main road and then call a Grab.
Even if entrance is free, facilities may have separate fees, so bring a little cash.
Even with plenty of shade the humidity is high, so bring water, a hat and mosquito repellent.
If you plan to use the pool, bring your own swimsuit and towel.
Weekends and holidays draw many families, so weekday mornings are recommended.
Traffic is heavy, so allow extra time when traveling from Ortigas.
Opening hours and closing days differ between sources, so check the official channel (Pasig City CENRO) before you visit.
Many areas forbid damaging animals or plants or feeding the animals, so follow the signs.
Checking the park's official social channels for event schedules and maintenance notices will reduce wasted trips.
Bring swim diapers, a change of clothes and water shoes for children.
Wear comfortable sneakers for walking. Paths are mostly paved, but some spots are slippery after rain.
Opening hours and facility fees differ greatly between sources, so always check the latest notice before you visit.
Adventure facilities such as the zipline and wall climbing have safety rules and age and weight limits. Follow the staff's instructions.
Watch for lost belongings even inside the park, and keep valuables on you.
In the rainy season it can rain suddenly and some facilities may close.
Some facilities may be closed for renovation or maintenance.
Some facilities have offered discounts to Pasig residents, so confirm the rate for foreigners.
The road outside the main gate is congested during rush hours. When you call a Grab, specify the pickup point exactly and check the license plate.
A business and shopping district about
15 to 30 minutes
away by car, good for continuing with a meal or shopping.
Central Pasig has churches, the city hall area and a riverside promenade worth seeing. Read the guide to the whole city as well to plan your day more easily.
A mixed-use commercial district on the Quezon City side with many cinemas and restaurants.
Marikina, close to Pasig, has a shoe museum and a riverside park.
